quote: Early studiers of cults were surprised to discover than when cults receive a major shock—a prophecy fails to come true, a moral flaw of the founder is revealed—they often come back stronger than before
content: Fable's own list of typical outcomes, "reinterpretation, quiet decline and schism," is what evaporative cooling predicts: the group shrinks, and those who remain hold the belief more firmly. The essay does not predict growth. It predicts that the average member left behind will be more fervent. Reviews of failed prophecy find that groups rarely dissolve and that the remaining members typically rationalize and hold on (Dawson 1999). Hardyck & Braden's group did not proselytize, and its members did not give up the belief either. Dorothy Martin went on teaching as "Sister Thedra" for decades. On 1975, the Society's own later statement acknowledged that its publications had raised expectations for that year (Watchtower, 15 March 1980). The post-1975 decline followed by a harder core is the essay's pattern in a single case.

quote: For that matter, I can’t recall seeing the evaporative cooling analogy elsewhere, though that doesn’t mean it hasn’t been noted before.
content: Hirschman is the right precedent, and the essay says it probably has one ("that doesn't mean it hasn't been noted before"). The two prescriptions differ, though, and the difference is the essay's contribution. Hirschman's remedy for firms is to raise the cost of exit so that quality-sensitive customers stay and use their voice. For a belief group, a high cost of exit is the cult's own method: isolation, shunning, surrendered savings. The essay prescribes the other lever, cheaper voice: "be prejudiced in favor of tolerating dissent," and keep the articulate critic who "legitimiz[es] less extreme disagreements." Applied to an epistemic community, Hirschman's firm-level advice would produce a worse outcome, and the essay avoids that. The applet illustrated a mechanism Hirschman did not have: the shift in the distribution of belief among those who remain.
